transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-09-14
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 71 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Alice Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Leila Park (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Cobalt), Jamal Ortiz (Cobalt), Elena Kuznetsova (Cobalt SRE), Ravi Menon (Cobalt)

Summary (auto): Quick recap, deep dive on prefetch heuristics; action items to exchange traces and run microbench.

[00:00] Alice Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining we'll keep this to an hour plus a bit, uh we're going to focus on the prefetch behavior you saw in your clusters and the tail spikes with TRT-LLM, and compare that to vLLM runs
[00:18] Priya Nair: yeah thanks Alice, we looked like 95th and 99th were fine but 99.9 just jumps, and it's not consistent across nodes.
[00:32] Marco Ruiz: that's the nonuniform prefetch pattern, so some requests trigger kv cold paths and that causes kernel switchups mid sequence, and with cudaGraph capture you can hit rebinds that add tens to hundreds of ms
[00:50] Jamal Ortiz: to be clear — we captured traces where it looks like a cudagraph replay mismatch? the capture size is different from replay size?
[01:05] Leila Park: sometimes the graph is captured with an optimistic kv layout, then when a request has extra prefetch it ends up doing a fallback path — which fires a different kernel and the scheduler stalls a bit, yes
[01:20] Elena Kuznetsova: our infra team is worried about bursty latencies — customers hit an SLA with 200ms tail and it spiked to 1.1s on a 4k token job
[01:34] Alice Chen: can you share that job profile, Ravi? the tokenization/response pattern matters, also whether you had kv warm or cold in the same session
[01:48] Ravi Menon: sending a link now — tiny noise in transcript: link/shared-drive/trace-0928 (post-meeting)
[02:00] Alice Chen: ok great, let's go into specifics. Marco, can you sketch what we instrumented in Redwood for the heuristic?
[02:12] Marco Ruiz: sure. we track per-model per-shard sequence-length distribution and maintain a histogram. heuristic picks either eager prefetch (aggressive kv fetch at start) or lazy prefetch (pull on demand). the problem is nonuniform workloads — some requests have long contexts suddenly interleaved with short ones which confuses the cudaGraph capture phase
[02:36] Jamal Ortiz: hmm so this is a cross-request phenomenon not just single-request perf? sounds like contention in the scheduler plus kernel path switch
[02:45] Marco Ruiz: exactly. when a cudaGraph was captured under a mostly short-ctx workload then a long-ctx request causes a kernel path that wasn't in the graph, we either fallback to host-side kernels or do a forced capture which stalls
[03:00] Priya Nair: and you saw this on TRT-LLM more than vLLM?
[03:07] Leila Park: yes in our internal tests TRT-LLM had slightly better median throughput but suffered more from graph replay mismatches when kv prefetch ordering changed. vLLM being more dynamic avoids the cudagraph rigidity but at slightly higher steady-state CPU/GPU utilization
[03:26] Jamal Ortiz: we noticed a pattern with quantized runs — 4-bit quant added another layer of kernel variants, so selection matrix explodes
[03:34] Marco Ruiz: correct; quantization increases kernel set, and the kernel selector may pick a different kernel depending on alignment and sequence length; that ups the chance of mismatch during cudaGraph replay
[03:46] Elena Kuznetsova: is there a practical mitigation? we can't rewrite all clients
[03:51] Marco Ruiz: a few levers — 1) conservative capture window: capture with a superset of expected behaviors (but cost is more memory and slightly higher capture time) 2) aggressive per-request capture (lower reuse) 3) hybrid prefetch: a small eager prefix then demand fetch 4) kernel set pruning / quant-profile consolidation
[04:13] Priya Nair: please unpack hybrid prefetch — Jamal, does that align with your observed traffic?
[04:19] Jamal Ortiz: in our traces roughly 40% of requests are short (<=128) and 10% are long (>=1024). if we did a tiny eager prefetch of say first 64 tokens, we avoid many on-path fallbacks and only do demand for the true long ones
[04:33] Marco Ruiz: right, that reduces variance. but watch for kv cache eviction: a too-large eager step can thrash the KV cache and hurt throughput for other concurrent requests
[04:45] Ravi Menon: can we see a microbench where you sweep eager size (0, 32, 64, 128) and watch 99.9?
[04:52] Alice Chen: yes we'll include that in the pilot harness. Tom note: microbench to be shared — (note: Tom not present)
[05:00] [05:00] Leila Park: quick aside — we also instrument kernel hotness and coalesce similar kernels during runtime. one trick is to canonicalize quant layouts so fewer kernel variants get generated
[05:15] Priya Nair: canonicalize? like convert all int4 to the same packing?
[05:20] Leila Park: packing/stride normalization, yes. sometimes models produce weights with different alignment; normalizing before serving reduces kernel explosion
[05:28] Jamal Ortiz: our team can't change model files in prod but we can run a preprocess step in infra — would Redwood support that in Private?
[05:36] Marco Ruiz: for Private yes, we can add a preprocessing pipeline. for Hosted we do that in the model onboarding step and it's optional
[05:43] Elena Kuznetsova: what about NVLink/multi-GPU? the repro we saw was worse on multi-gpu with NVLink because of asynchronous prefetch races
[05:53] Marco Ruiz: NVLink introduces ordering nondeterminism when prefetches cross devices; kernel choice plus cross-device comms can add jitter. that's why we test on single and multi-gpu nodes in microbench
[06:05] Ravi Menon: can you expand on where TRT-LLM specifically diverges vs vLLM from an engineer perspective?
[06:11] Marco Ruiz: TRT-LLM is heavily tuned for steady-state throughput using cudaGraph captures and static kernel graphs. vLLM is dynamic and uses async scheduling; it trades off slightly higher average utilization to remain flexible per-request. so in bursts or nonuniform contexts, vLLM's scheduler can avoid the graph mismatch penalty
[06:29] Alice Chen: quick reality check — customers often pick TRT variant for cost, but see tail spikes; some pick vLLM for stable tails with higher cost. we're trying to find a hybrid that gives cost without the tail SLO hit
[06:42] Priya Nair: SLO here is 200ms P99.9 for our interactive product — can't exceed that more than a few times an hour
[06:49] Marco Ruiz: understood. one more nuance: opaque fallbacks in TRT-LLM sometimes trigger host->device memcpy for a kernel we didn't anticipate and that kills latency because of stream synchronization
[07:03] Jamal Ortiz: we saw synchronous memcpy in nvprof, yep
[07:08] Leila Park: also, CUDA graph capture boundaries are sized by the runtime heuristics. if a capture occurs across a boundary where KV cache state changes mid-capture you get a mismatch; a mismatch forces a path that's not in graph resulting in thread-block differences
[07:26] Elena Kuznetsova: our ops team wants a concrete mitigation we can deploy quickly — is hybrid prefetch zero-touch?
[07:33] Marco Ruiz: hybrid needs a small runtime heuristic — can be configured at model route level. default is zero eager. we can push a safe default (eager 32) for latency-sensitive routes to evaluate
[07:44] Ravi Menon: and quantization? when we move to 4-bit, does kernel explosion make hybrid less effective?
[07:51] Marco Ruiz: increases complexity but hybrid still helps — it reduces the chance of encountering odd kernel combos early. combined with quant-profile consolidation it's effective
[08:03] Alice Chen: let's talk VPC/on-prem ramifications — Priya, you run on VPC with customer-managed nodes, right?
[08:10] Priya Nair: yes private deployment, limited ops window to install patches. we need clear, low-risk changes we can roll out in canaries
[08:18] Marco Ruiz: for Private we can provide a canary image with the runtime change (hybrid prefetch + canonicalization). you'd run it on a small pool and we monitor nvtx traces and tail metrics
[08:29] Jamal Ortiz: what about security and compliance? we can't forward traces with PII out of our VPC
[08:36] Alice Chen: understood — we can accept redacted traces or run a short consultant session with your team in your VPC. Redwood Private includes options to do on-prem instrumentation collection under NDA
[08:48] Elena Kuznetsova: acceptable, thanks
[08:52] [08:52] Marco Ruiz: diving deeper: here's a cause we found — prefetch ordering mismatches produce kernel schedule divergence where the next op's workspace allocation differs, producing a different kernel launch config which isn't in the capture; the runtime then either recreates graph or executes fallback kernels synchronously
[09:14] Jamal Ortiz: so the root cause is the allocation / alignment differences that change grid/block dims?
[09:20] Marco Ruiz: yes, alignment and lane packing. quantized kernels are especially sensitive because packing affects shared memory usage and block size heuristics
[09:30] Leila Park: to add, the launch config can change also with local batch coalescing — when multiple small requests are coalesced, kernel config differs from single request case
[09:41] Ravi Menon: is there a way to force a canonical launch config so kernel choice remains stable? even if suboptimal sometimes?
[09:49] Marco Ruiz: you can clamp to conservative config which reduces throughput slightly but stabilizes the tail; it's a classic latency vs throughput tradeoff
[09:58] Priya Nair: show us numbers — conservative clamp cost vs tail improvement
[10:02] Leila Park: in our evals we saw median drop 5-8% but 99.9 improved by 60-80% in offending cases
[10:12] Jamal Ortiz: that's compelling if our SLA is at risk
[10:15] Marco Ruiz: we'll include that clamp sweep in the microbench (clamp values, eager size, capture window)
[10:22] Alice Chen: switch topic briefly — telemetry: what traces do you already have?
[10:27] Ravi Menon: we've uploaded top-level NVTX traces, logs showing memcpy spikes, and a small sample of cudagraph capture markers. we didn't include raw kernel names due to size
[10:37] Marco Ruiz: we need full kernel names, block/grid, sm occupancy samples. nvprof/Nsight report is best. we'll provide a small script to compress and redact PII
[10:47] Priya Nair: please make the script in our VPC — can't send raw traces off premise
[10:52] Marco Ruiz: yes we can provide a containerized trace collector that runs in your VPC and uploads only metadata you approve
[11:00] Elena Kuznetsova: timeline?
[11:03] Alice Chen: we proposed traces by 9/18 and microbench repo by 9/17. Does that fit?
[11:10] Jamal Ortiz: yes we'll aim for that
[11:13] [11:13] Marco Ruiz: note on CUDA graph capture strategies — some teams capture multiple graphs for different sequence-length buckets to avoid cross-bucket mismatches; downside is more memory and less reuse but fewer mismatches
[11:31] Leila Park: alternative is dynamic recomposition — detect mismatch and incrementally recompose graph rather than full recapture, which can be faster but is complex to implement across quant kernels
[11:44] Priya Nair: do you have a reference implementation?
[11:48] Marco Ruiz: partial; we'll link a prototype in the microbench repo. it's experimental and we advise testing in a canary pool
[11:56] Ravi Menon: for the pilot can we limit to single-node first? multi-gpu adds NVLink nondeterminism that may mask the effect
[12:04] Alice Chen: yes single-node single-gpu then escalate to nvlink nodes after we baseline
[12:10] Jamal Ortiz: one more concern — model parallelism frameworks can also introduce fragmentation; we use a sharded approach for one model — will that break the canonicalization?
[12:19] Marco Ruiz: it can. canonicalization must operate per-shard with shard-aware packing. we'll document guidelines for that in the pilot scope
[12:30] [12:30] Leila Park: operational note — the runtime will emit a mismatch event metric; we recommend adding that to your alerting to catch regressions quickly
[12:38] Elena Kuznetsova: good — we want alert thresholds on mismatch count per minute
[12:43] Alice Chen: ok near the end here, let's summarize next steps and owners
[12:48] Alice Chen: action items recap: Redwood share microbench + trace collector, Cobalt run baseline, both exchange results, follow-up review meeting
[13:00] Priya Nair: sounds good — any other questions?
[13:05] Marco Ruiz: small note — in some cases TensorRT still wins on cost for high steady-state throughput; the pilot should quantify cost delta for the clamp/hybrid options
[13:19] Ravi Menon: agreed we'll want cost/latency tradeoff table
[13:24] Alice Chen: final — we'll schedule follow-up, thanks all
[13:29] End meeting
